items.title: Marian McPartland — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I met Oscar . . . I think somewhere back yesterday I mentioned Jimmy and I played in Toronto in maybe the end of the ’40s or 1950.

ctx.x: I’m not surprised. As you said, that was the case. I’m sure each group, as you said, salaries varied from a contingent on how effective their agents and representatives were. Something else along those lines I was going to ask you was, you mentioned about six-day weeks . . . How many sets would that be per night? On average.

I think maybe it was about four. It was half an hour on and half an hour off. I think we started 9:00 to . . . I think we played 9:00 ’til 3:00, I’m pretty sure. There was a girl piano player who would play the intermissions. She would start . . . It was either 8:30 or 9:00. I know we went ’til 3:00, but I . . . We would seriously screw up the schedule, because we were just across from Birdland. We would get off after the . . . it would be a half an hour on and half an hour off. We’d go running over there if it…
So Duke and Oscar both sat in with your trio?

items.title: Marian McPartland interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, April 26, 1997
items.q: all kinds of people came in to Hickory House — Benny Goodman, Oscar Peterson, well you name it.

ctx.x: I like that phrase “arranger’s piano” actually. I think I’ll probably borrow that. It’s a compliment and it’s a qualifier too.

Well it’s sort of lets you know that it’s not an Oscar Peterson piano player. But nevertheless, Benny really played very well. And there’s other people you could qualify that way, like Gerry Mulligan. He’s another one and he definitely, I know he wanted to play the piano. He said the same thing and he left his horn on the kitchen table.
They probably wanted to get to play with you, you know, see what that felt like.
